title: Token-bucket admission + KV tiering + work-stealing scheduler cleanup
creator: Alex Kim
description: This ticket consolidates three related tech-debt efforts into a single coordinated refactor: (1) replace the current continuous-batcher admission policy with a token-bucket based admission controller to reduce head-of-line blocking; (2) introduce a hot/warm/cold tiering layer in the KV cache so that large KV footprints do not degrade tail latency; (3) replace the custom round-robin scheduler codepath with a work-stealing executor to improve CPU utilization and reduce long-tail stalls. Goal: simplify reasoning about admission/backpressure, reduce 95th/99th percentile latency variance, and make the cache lifecycle explicit for operational tuning.
background: Our serving runtime has accumulated overlapping ad-hoc backpressure and cache heuristics over several projects. Continuous batching logic intermixes admission, coalescing, and prefetch hooks in the same module; the KV cache is a flat LRU-like store that stores everything on a single tier; the scheduler uses coarse lane-based allocation and periodically stalls under imbalanced workloads. Recent incidents showed spikes in tail latency when large KV working sets were loaded and when a single model with long sequences monopolized worker lanes. Several prior tickets addressed slices of the problem (slot prewarm, lease coordinator), but we need a cohesive design to avoid repeated patches.
proposal:
- Implement token-bucket admission at ingress: each model-route and client-tier has a token bucket configured by throughput SLO. Tokens are refilled on a time window to smooth bursts. Requests that cannot acquire tokens within a short timeout are rejected or routed to a lower-cost fallback model.
- Introduce explicit KV cache tiers: hot (in-memory, pinned), warm (in-memory, probabilistic sampling), cold (on-disk mmap with async promotors). Add async populators and background demotion to avoid blocking the critical path.
- Replace lane-based round-robin scheduler with a work-stealing executor: per-worker deques with steal-on-empty semantics. This reduces global contention and provides better latency isolation for long-running tasks.
- Provide a compatibility shim so existing instrumentation and lease/heartbeat logic keeps working during rollout.
technical_design:
Key components:
1) Admission controller (token-bucket):
   - Config: tokens_per_sec, burst_capacity, acquire_timeout_ms, fallback_policy.
   - Fast-path: try_acquire() is a single atomic op; if success, request proceeds to batching.
   - Slow-path: if token unavailable, consult fallback policy (queue short wait, drop, or route-to-fallback-model).
2) KV tiering:
   - Hot: ~small set of pinned entries with fast eviction hooks; used for popular prefixes and cache hotkeys.
   - Warm: compacted in-memory region with probabilistic admission; LRU windowing; async promotors sample incoming access and elevate to hot.
   - Cold: memory-mapped backing store for full entries; async read-ahead for predicted next-token accesses.
   - API: tiered_get(key) returns a status (HIT_HOT/HIT_WARM/HIT_COLD/MISS) + latency hints for SLO attribution.
3) Work-stealing scheduler:
   - Per-worker deque, push/pop local; pop-bottom, steal-top.
   - Long-running CPU-bound tasks tagged so workers avoid stealing unless idle threshold reached.
   - Integrate with existing slot/lease system via a thin adapter that converts slot leases into task tokens.
4) Observability:
   - New metrics: token_acquire_latency_ms, admission_rejections, kv_tier_hit_rate_{hot,warm,cold}, steal_ops, worker_idle_time.
   - Trace spans: admission.acquire, kv.tier_lookup, scheduler.steal_attempt.
5) Config and rollout: feature-flagged per-cluster and per-model.
migration_plan:
Phased rollout to minimize risk:
- Phase 0 (lab): implement modules behind flags; unit tests and integration tests.
- Phase 1 (canary): enable token-bucket admission only for non-critical routes with detailed metrics. Monitor rejection rates and latency.
- Phase 2 (cache tiering): enable warm-tier reads for a controlled subset of models, keep promotors conservative.
- Phase 3 (scheduler): enable work-stealing on a small set of worker pools; run with a compatibility shim for lease/slot accounting.
- Phase 4: full switch, deprecate legacy code. Rollback plan: flags to revert each component; circuit-breakers for admission fallback.
benchmarks:
Baseline synthetic (mixed short/long sequences):
 - p50 token gen latency: 45ms
 - p95: 320ms
 - p99: 1.2s
After lab changes (token-bucket + warm-tier reads) on a small cluster:
 - p50: 44ms
 - p95: 220ms (improvement ~31%)
 - p99: 760ms (improvement ~37%)
Work-stealing reduced CPU tail stalling by ~20% in stress tests. Full cluster numbers TBD during canary. Bench harness and raw results stored at: https://confluence.redwoodinfra/internal/serving/ENG-271828/benchmarks
decisions:
- Use token-bucket (leaky-bucket alternative considered but token-bucket chosen for better burst control).
- Implement KV tiers in-process with mmap cold tier; ruled out external cache service to avoid network variability.
- Work-stealing chosen over coroutine-based green scheduling to keep compatibility with existing native code paths.
- Metrics and traces added up-front to allow SLO alerting during canary.
open_questions:
- Optimal hot-tier size heuristics: should we auto-scale per-model or centralize?
- How aggressive should the warm->hot promotion policy be to avoid thrashing?
- Integration with Dedicated: are cluster-level token budgets appropriate for reserved capacity customers?
- SSO/security review for mmap cold tier storing partial secrets (pending sec review).
acceptance_criteria:
- Token-bucket admission implemented and feature-flagged.
- KV tiering implemented with metrics emitting tier hit rates.
- Work-stealing scheduler adapter passes integration tests and shows no regression in p50/p95 for baseline routes.
- Canary passes for at least 72 hours with stable error budget and no >10% increase in client-facing errors.
- Documentation updated (Runbook + Confluence) and runbook drills rehearsed.
risks:
- Misconfigured token buckets may increase client errors; mitigate via conservative defaults and short acquire timeouts.
- KV tiering introduces complexity and potential correctness bugs (staleness) — add strict invariants and tests.
- Scheduler change could reveal hidden assumptions; maintain compatibility shim and slow rollout.
